01.note: Rabban Gamliel sat on a step on the Temple Mount with Yohanan the scribe standing before him and three blank sheets of parchment ready. He dictated three letters. The first two told the people of the Galilee and of the South that the time had come to clear out tithes still in their possession, from the olive vats and from the stacks of grain. The third told the Jews of Babylonia, Media and the rest of the Diaspora that the young birds were still tender, the lambs thin and spring not yet come, so 'it seemed good to me and to my colleagues' to add thirty days to the year.
01.why: The Gemara contrasts the stern earlier leaders with the humble later ones, and this letter shows Rabban Gamliel adding thirty days. Because he mentions his colleagues, the Gemara suggests he wrote it after he had been deposed and had to share his office.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader of the Sages, who dictates the official letters

people.name: Yoḥanan
people.about: The scribe who stands before Rabban Gamliel and writes the letters

terms.meaning: The duty, at set points in the seven-year farming cycle, to hand over or remove tithes that were set aside from produce but never given to the people they belong to.

terms.term: Adding thirty days to the year
terms.meaning: Intercalation: inserting an extra month so the calendar of festivals stays in step with the spring season.

02.note: During a time of Roman persecution, the Sages of the Land of Israel sent Rava a message in code. A pair of scholars had set out from Rakkath and been seized by 'the eagle', the Roman soldiers, while carrying 'items made in Luz', which the Gemara explains was sky-blue dye. By divine mercy and their own merit they came out safely. The 'offspring of Nahshon' had wanted to 'establish a pillar', that is, add a month to the year, but 'that Edomite', the Roman governor, would not let them. Even so, the assembly gathered and established it in the month in which Aaron the priest died.
02.why: A teaching says the court may not add a month to the year before Rosh HaShana. The Gemara cites this message as a case where it was done in summer; it answers that the court may calculate early but may not announce it until after Rosh HaShana.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage in Babylonia to whom the coded message was sent

terms.meaning: A rare blue dye needed for the ritual fringes on a garment's corners; here it is smuggled goods the scholars were carrying.
Code for adding an extra month to the year, so that the festivals stay in their proper season.

terms.term: The month in which Aaron died
terms.meaning: Code for the summer month of Av, before the new year.

03.note: Rav says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava should be remembered favorably: without him, the laws of fines would have ceased in Israel. The Roman government once decreed that anyone who ordained a judge would be killed, anyone ordained would be killed, the town where it happened destroyed and its boundaries uprooted. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava went out to a spot between two mountains and two towns, between Usha and Shefaram, and there ordained five elders, among them Rabbi Meir. When their enemies found them he told them, 'My sons, run.' They asked what would become of him; he said he lay before the Romans like a stone no one could overturn. The soldiers did not leave until they had driven three hundred iron spears into him, leaving him like a sieve.
03.why: A teaching says ordination needs three judges, and the Gemara asks whether one man could ordain. This story seems to show one man doing it; the Gemara replies that others may have been with him and were left unnamed out of respect for him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: An elderly Sage who ordained five students despite the Roman decree, and was killed for it

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of the five elders he ordained

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who says Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava should be remembered favorably

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, giving a Sage authority to judge cases such as fines.
Penalties set by the Torah that only properly ordained judges could impose.
The limit around a town beyond which one may not walk on Shabbat; he sat between two such limits so that no town could be blamed.

04.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan kept trying to ordain Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Hoshaya, but something always got in the way, and he was very upset about it. The two of them told him not to be upset: they were descended from the house of Eli.
04.why: The Gemara has been discussing who may be ordained and where. This story leads to Rabbi Yonatan's teaching, from the curse on Eli's house, that his descendants are never to be ordained.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A teacher who repeatedly tries and fails to ordain the two Sages

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Yoḥanan wanted to ordain

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi Yoḥanan wanted to ordain

people.name: Eli
people.about: The High Priest from whom the two Sages say they descend

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, which gives a Sage authority to judge.

05.note: Rabbi Zeira used to hide so that he would not be ordained, because Rabbi Elazar taught: stay obscure and stay alive. When he heard Rabbi Elazar's other teaching, that no one rises to greatness unless all his sins are forgiven, he presented himself for ordination. At his ordination the Sages sang him a wedding song for a bride: no eye shadow, no rouge, no hair dye, and still she is full of grace. When Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were ordained, they sang: ordain for us anyone like these, but not the worthless or the twisters of the law (or, in another version, not robbers or bullies).
05.why: This is one of a run of ordination stories in the discussion. The songs sung at these ceremonies lead the Gemara on to the song the women of the emperor's house sang for Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who first avoided ordination, then sought it

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage whose two sayings changed Rabbi Zeira's mind

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage ordained together with Rabbi Asi

people.name: Rabbi Asi

06.note: At first, when people comforted mourners, the mourners stood in place and everyone else filed past them. But two families in Jerusalem kept fighting over this, each insisting, 'We pass first.' So the Sages decreed that the people should stand and the mourners should pass by them.
06.why: Rav Pappa has just learned from a teaching about the High Priest that mourners stand while the people pass. This teaching explains why that custom was once reversed; the Gemara then adds that Rabbi Yosei later restored it in Tzippori.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

07.note: A slave of King Yannai killed a man. Shimon ben Shataḥ told the Sages to put the king on trial. They sent word to Yannai, who sent them the slave; they replied that he must come too, since the Torah says the owner of an ox that kills must stand with his ox. Yannai came and sat down. Shimon ben Shataḥ told him to stand, for he stood before the One who spoke and the world came into being. Yannai said he would stand only if the other judges told him to. Shimon ben Shataḥ turned right and left, and the judges stared at the ground in silence. He said, 'You are masters of thoughts; may the Master of thoughts come and punish you.' At once the angel Gabriel struck them to the ground and they died. Then the Sages ruled that a king neither judges nor is judged.
07.why: The mishna says a king does not judge and is not judged, and Rav Yosef limits this to the kings of Israel, not the house of David. The Gemara asks why those kings are exempt and answers with this incident.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: The king whose slave killed a man, summoned to court

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The Sage who insists the king stand trial

people.name: Gabriel
people.about: The angel who strikes down the silent judges

08.note: A certain slaughterer was found to have sold meat from an animal that was not kosher. Rav Naḥman disqualified him as a witness and removed him from his post. The man went and let his fingernails and hair grow long, as a sign of remorse, and Rav Naḥman thought of reinstating him. Rava said to him: perhaps he is only putting on a show. The story does not say what Rav Naḥman decided.
08.why: The discussion is about who is disqualified as a witness. After Rava's doubt, the Gemara asks how such a man can prove he has changed, and answers with Rav Idi bar Avin's test: he must give up something valuable in a place where nobody knows him.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who removed the slaughterer and then considered reinstating him

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who suspects the man's repentance is a trick

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is forbidden even if it was slaughtered properly.
The trained person who kills animals in the ritual way, and whom buyers trust to sell only permitted meat.

09.note: Rabbi Zeira's father collected taxes for thirteen years. Whenever the chief tax collector of the region came to town, he warned the rabbis with a verse from Isaiah: 'Come, my people, enter your chambers.' To the townspeople he said that the chief collector was coming and would now slaughter father before son and son before father. Everyone hid, and when the chief arrived he asked him, 'From whom shall I collect?' On his deathbed he told those around him to take thirteen coins tied in his sheet and return them to a certain man: he had taken them from him and had not needed them.
09.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that an ordinary tax collector may serve as a witness unless he is known to collect more than people owe. This story shows a tax collector who protected his town and gave back money he took without need.

people.name: The father of Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A tax collector who shielded his town and returned money on his deathbed

terms.meaning: The chief tax collector over the region, who came to town to collect.
A small silver coin.

10.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zarnokei and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak were travelling to Asya to add a month to the year, and Reish Lakish joined them to watch. Twice in the Sabbatical Year he saw a man working a field, once pruning vines and once plowing, and each time he exclaimed, 'A priest!' Each time the two offered an excuse for the man, and he rejected one of them: 'The heart knows whether it is for a bale or for deceit.' Calling him a nuisance, they climbed a roof and pulled the ladder away so he could not follow. Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yoḥanan whether such men could set the calendar, calling them a conspiracy of the wicked; Rabbi Yoḥanan said this was troubling. When the two complained that Reish Lakish had called them cattle herders, he said 'shepherds' would not have been too harsh.
10.why: The Gemara has explained how heavy Roman taxes led the Sages to go easier on those who gather produce in the Sabbatical Year. Reish Lakish's phrase leads the Gemara to ask where the rule that a conspiracy of the wicked is not counted comes from.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who joins the trip and objects to the travellers' leniency

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Zarnokei
people.about: One of the two Sages sent to add a month to the year

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
people.about: The other Sage sent to add a month to the year

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The teacher whom both sides come to

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when fields in the Land of Israel must lie fallow and may not be plowed or pruned.

terms.term: Adding a month to the year
terms.meaning: Intercalation: inserting an extra month so the festivals stay in their season; only qualified Sages could decide it.
The Gemara explains that priests were suspected of disregarding the Sabbatical Year, so Reish Lakish assumed the workers were priests.
Earlier the Gemara noted that cattle herders know nothing of law, and that ordinary shepherds may not serve as witnesses, so both were insults.

11.note: Some gravediggers buried a body on the first day of the festival of Shavuot. Rav Pappa excommunicated them and disqualified them as witnesses, but Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, declared them fit. Rav Pappa asked: aren't they wicked? Rav Huna answered that they thought they were doing a good deed. Rav Pappa asked: but I excommunicated them! Rav Huna answered that they thought the Sages were giving them atonement, not condemning them.
11.why: Rav Naḥman has just said that one who steals at harvest time is not called a thief and remains a valid witness. This case asks the same thing about people who broke the law believing they were doing right.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who excommunicated and disqualified the gravediggers

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who declared the gravediggers fit to testify

terms.meaning: Placed under a ban that cut a person off from the community until he changed his ways.
A festival day on which, like Shabbat, most work is forbidden.
A commandment or good deed; burying the dead is a major one.

12.note: A man named bar Ḥama killed a person. The Exilarch told Rav Abba bar Ya'akov to investigate and, if bar Ḥama had certainly killed him, to have his eyes put out. Two witnesses testified that he had. Bar Ḥama brought two witnesses against one of them: one said he had seen him steal a measure of barley, the other a spear handle. Rav Abba bar Ya'akov objected that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who lets a man caught out in money matters still testify in capital cases. Rav Pappi answered that this does not hold where an unnamed teaching follows Rabbi Meir, as one does here. The Gemara works out which teaching he meant. One witness was disqualified and bar Ḥama went free; he kissed Rav Pappi's feet and took on paying his tax for the rest of his life.
12.why: The Gemara has ruled that a witness who has done monetary wrong is disqualified even in capital cases, because an unnamed mishna follows Rabbi Meir. Asked where that mishna is, it answers with this case.

people.name: Bar Ḥama
people.about: A man accused of killing a person, who discredits a witness against him

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Babylonian Jewish community, who orders the investigation

people.name: Rav Abba bar Ya'akov
people.about: The Sage sent to investigate

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: The Sage whose argument gets bar Ḥama acquitted

terms.meaning: A teaching in the Mishna given without a Sage's name; the law usually follows it, so it can settle a dispute between named Sages.
A dry measure, a few liters.
Trials where the defendant's life or body is at stake, as opposed to cases about money.

13.note: Rav came to a certain place to buy parchment, and the people there asked him whether a man may testify about his stepson's wife. Two versions of his answer survive. In Sura they say he answered that a husband is like his wife, so the stepson's wife counts as the man's daughter-in-law. In Pumbedita they say he answered that a wife is like her husband, so she counts as his stepson; Rav Huna, quoting Rav Naḥman, finds this in the Torah's calling an uncle's wife 'your aunt'.
13.why: The discussion is listing which relatives by marriage may not testify about one another, case by case. This question adds one more such relationship.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who is asked the question while buying parchment

terms.meaning: Two Babylonian centres of learning; each preserves its own version of Rav's answer.

14.note: Two brothers-in-law had signed as witnesses on a deed of gift. Rav Yosef was ready to declare it valid, since Shmuel ruled the law follows Rabbi Yosei, who allows brothers-in-law. Abaye asked how he knew Shmuel did not mean another version of Rabbi Yosei, who disqualifies them. Rav Yosef cited Shmuel's own words, 'like Pineḥas and me', who were brothers as well as brothers-in-law, so ordinary brothers-in-law must be fine. Abaye replied that Shmuel may have meant the in-law tie alone. So Rav Yosef told the holder of the deed to acquire the gift through the witnesses who watched it handed over, following Rabbi Elazar. The story stops before saying whether that worked.
14.why: Shmuel has just ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, but Rabbi Yosei's view is reported in two forms, in the mishna and in a teaching outside it. This case shows a judge forced to decide which one Shmuel meant.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The judge deciding whether the deed is valid

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who challenges Rav Yosef's reasoning

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The authority whose ruling Rav Yosef relies on

people.name: Pineḥas
people.about: Shmuel's brother, who was also his brother-in-law

terms.meaning: A signed document transferring property to someone as a gift.

terms.term: Witnesses who watched it handed over
terms.meaning: According to Rabbi Elazar, these witnesses make the transfer valid; the signatures only add authority.

14.flag: The story stops at Rav Yosef's instruction; its ending (Abaye's further objection and Rav Yosef saying 'go away, they won't let me give it to you') is in the AFTER segment.

15.note: Mar Ukva's brothers-in-law had been his relatives by marriage, but that tie had ended. When they came before him for judgment, he said he was disqualified from judging them. They asked whether he was following Rabbi Yehuda, and offered to bring a letter from the Land of Israel saying the law does not follow him. Mar Ukva answered, 'Am I stuck to you with a measure of wax?' He agreed they were no longer relatives; he was stepping aside only because they would not obey his verdict.
15.why: The Gemara has just reported rulings that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who says a former in-law with children from the marriage stays disqualified. Mar Ukva's case shows a judge who accepts this and still steps aside for another reason.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A judge who refuses to hear his former brothers-in-law's case

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel, seen from Babylonia.

terms.term: Stuck with a measure of wax
terms.meaning: An expression: do you think I am glued to you? He means he is no longer related to them.

16.note: A miser people called 'a mouse lying on dinars' said on his deathbed that certain men had money claims against him. After he died they sued his heirs. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, ruled that while a man may lie about debts during his life so as not to look rich, on his deathbed he is believed. The heirs paid half. When the claimants sued for the other half before Rabbi Ḥiyya, he said a man may also lie so that his sons will not look rich. The heirs asked to go back and undo the first payment; Rabbi Ḥiyya said, 'The elder has already ruled.'
16.why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that a person's loose talk about owing money does not bind him, because people say such things so as not to look rich. This case asks whether that holds for words spoken on a deathbed.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The first judge, who holds the heirs liable

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The second judge, who disagrees but will not overturn the elder's ruling

terms.meaning: Coins; the nickname mocks a man who sat on his money without using it.

17.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim had tried without success to get Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, ordained. One day Rabbi Yoḥanan asked his students whether anyone knew if the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa. Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim said his friend knew, and asked Rabbi Yoḥanan to ordain him first. Rabbi Yoḥanan did, then asked what he had heard. He said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa agrees with Rabbi Natan. Disappointed, Rabbi Yoḥanan said, 'For this I needed him?' since it was obvious. Still he told him, 'Since you have gone up, you will not come down.' Rabbi Zeira concluded that once a great man is ordained, the ordination stands.
17.why: The discussion is whether two witnesses must see an event and testify together, a dispute between Rabbi Natan, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa and others. The story turns on that question, and the Gemara then gives Rav's ruling on it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
people.about: A Sage who manoeuvres to get his friend ordained

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage who is ordained and reports the teaching

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The teacher who ordains him and is let down by the answer

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who draws a rule from the incident

terms.meaning: The formal granting of the title Rabbi, which gives a Sage authority to judge.
That two witnesses need not have seen the event together for their testimony to be combined.

18.note: A rumor spread about a certain student that he had revealed something said in confidence in the study hall, twenty-two years earlier. Rav Ami expelled him from the study hall, saying, 'This one is a revealer of secrets.'
18.why: A teaching forbids a judge to tell a litigant that he voted to acquit but was outvoted, citing the verse about a talebearer who reveals secrets. Rav Ami's act shows how seriously such disclosure was taken, even decades later.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: The Sage who expels the student

terms.meaning: The house of learning where the Sages discussed and taught Torah.

19.note: A child was brought to court before Rav Naḥman. Asked whether he had witnesses, he said no; asked whether he had any evidence, he said no; and Rav Naḥman ruled against him. As the child walked off crying, some people heard him and said, 'We know about your father's affairs.' Rav Naḥman ruled that in such a case even the Rabbis agree their testimony is accepted, since a child does not know his father's business.
19.why: The mishna says that if someone declared he had no witnesses and then produced some, they are worthless, and the law follows the Rabbis on this. Rav Naḥman's case marks the limit of that rule: it does not apply to a child.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who first rules against the child, then accepts his witnesses

terms.meaning: Here, the majority of Sages in the mishna, who say late witnesses are not accepted once a litigant has said he has none.

20.note: A woman was holding a promissory note on someone's behalf, and she said she knew it had been repaid. Rav Naḥman believed her. Rava asked whether this was because Rabbi held that handing over a note transfers ownership; Rav Naḥman said no, she was believed because she could have burned it. In another version Rav Naḥman did not believe her, and when Rava said she could have burned it, he answered that once a note has been confirmed in court that argument no longer works. Rava challenged him with a teaching that a receipt held by a trustee is valid. The Gemara concludes that Rav Naḥman's view is refuted.
20.why: It comes right after another of Rav Naḥman's rulings on whose testimony a court accepts, in the discussion of the mishna on new evidence after a verdict.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who rules on the woman's claim

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who questions and finally refutes Rav Naḥman

terms.meaning: A signed document recording a loan, which the lender can use to collect.
A note whose witnesses' signatures the court has verified, giving it full legal force.
A neutral third party who holds a document for two sides.
